The bill would close gaps in Australia's foreign intelligence warrant framework so agencies can better collect intelligence on foreign threats.

It would allow the Director-General of Security to seek warrants for intercepting communications to obtain foreign intelligence, even when the geographic location of the sender and recipient cannot be determined beforehand.
The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security would review the amendments five years after the bill starts.
Amends the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Act 1979.
Removes the strict ban on intercepting domestic communications that both start and end within Australia.
Allows the Attorney-General to issue warrants for collecting foreign intelligence on Australians in Australia who act for a foreign power.
Intelligence agencies, the Director-General of Security, the Attorney-General, the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, and Australians acting for foreign powers.
Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 - Second Reading - Agree with bill's main idea

The government argued the Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 is needed to close two gaps: allowing ASIO to collect foreign communications without knowing the geographic location, and enabling continued intelligence collection on Australians acting for foreign powers when they return to Australia. Robust safeguards, including mandatory destruction of incidentally collected domestic communications and oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, were outlined.
Presented the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security's advisory report on the Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021.

The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security presented its advisory report on the Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021, recommending amendments that include notifying the committee if a mandatory written procedure is issued or varied and a review at least five years after royal assent; subject to those amendments, the committee recommended the bill's passage to allow warrants for intercepting foreign communications while prohibiting domestic interception.

The Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 amends the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 and the ASIO Act 1979 to address gaps in the foreign intelligence warrant framework caused by technological change, ensuring alignment with Five Eyes partners while maintaining safeguards including a prohibition on collecting domestic communications. The bill enables warrants for foreign intelligence collection on Australians acting for foreign powers and introduces mandatory screening and destruction procedures for inadvertently intercepted domestic communications.

The Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 updates foreign communications warrants to reflect technological changes and allows foreign intelligence warrants for Australians acting on behalf of a foreign power, with oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security. The government accepted all recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security's report tabled on 25 August 2021.
Crossbench members received no briefing, explanatory memorandum, or opportunity to consider the Foreign Intelligence Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 before it passed the House.

The bill introduces a new annual charge on all higher education providers registered with TEQSA to recover the costs of its risk monitoring and regulatory oversight activities, with the amount to be set by regulations. The charge will be phased in from 1 January 2022 (20% of costs in 2022, 50% in 2023, 100% in 2024) and is expected to collect around $5.7 million annually, replacing the current partial recovery of about 15% of TEQSA's total costs.

The bills increase TEQSA's cost recovery from about 15% to full cost through higher application fees (from 1 January 2022) and a new annual charge phased in at 20% in 2022, 50% in 2023 and 100% in 2024, originally announced in the 2018–19 budget but delayed due to COVID-19.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and the amendment bill, arguing that higher education providers should pay increased cost recovery fees—phased in over three years—to fund TEQSA’s regulatory activities, noting that current cost recovery is about 15% and that the sector had $38 billion in revenue in 2017.

Labor opposes the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021, arguing that the cost‑recovery measure unfairly burdens a higher education sector already devastated by 17,000 job losses, a 10% real funding cut over three years, soaring student debt of $60,000, and a government‑driven brain drain of researchers.

The speaker supported the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (Charges) Bill 2021 and related amendment, which phase in increased cost recovery for TEQSA from 15% to full cost by 2024, and noted $245 million in federal funding for Edith Cowan University's new Perth campus, set to open in 2025 with $695 million total cost.

The speaker argued for passing the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency cost recovery bills, with fee waivers during COVID and a three-year transition from 2022; they cited $1.5 billion in additional support for public universities, $53 million for private providers, and rebutted opposition claims by stating no public university met JobSeeker eligibility thresholds (30% revenue decline) and that several universities—including Monash ($267M surplus), Melbourne ($178M), Flinders ($35M), USQ ($12M), and Western Sydney ($13M)—reported surpluses in 2020.

Labor supported extending virtual AGMs until 16 September 2021 but opposed Schedule 2, arguing it would permanently weaken continuous disclosure and misleading-conduct laws by making directors liable only for knowing, reckless or negligent failures, citing a King & Wood Mallesons survey in which only 21.5% of executives favoured making the changes permanent and opposition from the Australian Shareholders Association. The member moved a second reading amendment noting the measures would strip shareholders' rights, damage corporate governance, and hurt Australian investment and retirees, and foreshadowed an amendment to separate the two schedules.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 undermines shareholder democracy and accountability by making permanent a weakened continuous disclosure regime, which only holds directors liable for non-disclosure if they acted with knowledge, recklessness or negligence. They supported Schedule 1’s temporary extension of virtual AGMs due to COVID-19, but opposed Schedule 2, citing opposition from the Australian Shareholders' Association and the Australian Council of Superannuation Investors.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 extends temporary relief for companies to hold virtual meetings and execute documents until 15 September 2021, and permanently introduces a fault element of knowledge, recklessness or negligence for continuous disclosure civil penalty proceedings to reduce opportunistic class actions.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021 extends temporary relief allowing companies to use technology for meetings, document execution, and distribution until 15 September 2021, with permanent reforms for electronic signing and materials, plus a pilot for hybrid annual general meetings.

Labor opposed schedule 2 of the bill, which would permanently weaken continuous disclosure obligations by requiring shareholders to prove directors had knowledge or were reckless before suing, and cited only 10 shareholder class actions in 2019 to counter the government's claim of opportunistic litigation.

The Labor speaker argued that the Morrison government's Treasury Laws Amendment Bill would undermine shareholders' rights by weakening continuous disclosure laws, citing a King & Wood Mallesons survey where only 11.3% of company directors used the temporary changes and nearly 80% opposed making them permanent, while also accusing the government of punishing transparency, referencing the sports rorts affair and Auditor-General budget cuts.

The Greens oppose schedule 2 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (2021 Measures No. 1) Bill 2021, arguing it would reverse the burden of proof in continuous disclosure laws, enable insider trading, and benefit large corporations and billionaires at the expense of ordinary shareholders and investors. The speaker also criticised the government for cutting JobSeeker and JobKeeper supports while weakening corporate transparency.

The speaker argued that the government's Treasury Laws Amendment Bill permanently weakens Australia's continuous disclosure regime, making it easier for company directors to withhold price-sensitive information from shareholders. The speaker called for the bill to be split, allowing temporary virtual AGM provisions (Schedule 1) to pass while subjecting the permanent disclosure changes (Schedule 2) to proper Senate inquiry, citing opposition from the Australian Shareholders Association and a survey where over 80% of executives opposed making the temporary changes permanent.

The bill’s second schedule, which would permanently weaken continuous disclosure and misleading conduct provisions, was opposed, while the temporary extension of virtual AGMs was supported. The government was accused of hypocrisy for cutting JobKeeper while retaining business relief, and opposition from ASIC, the Australian Shareholders Association, and 80% of surveyed executives was noted.

The speaker argued against the Treasury Laws Amendment Bill, warning it enables a "creep" of reduced accountability and transparency in government, citing stonewalling on freedom-of-information requests and ministers avoiding direct answers by taking questions on notice.

The Government extended temporary COVID-19 relief allowing virtual company meetings and electronic document execution, with permanent reforms and a hybrid AGM pilot to follow. It also amended continuous disclosure laws so that companies and officers face civil penalties only when acting with knowledge, recklessness or negligence.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 is deeply flawed, particularly its stapling provisions that could default three million workers into underperforming funds and its unprecedented directions power giving the Treasurer authority to cancel private sector investments. Labor will move amendments to prevent stapling to underperforming funds and to reject the directions power.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 unfairly targets industry super funds, which have outperformed retail funds (30% asset growth since 2018 versus 3.2%), and that Labor is seeking amendments to protect workers' retirement savings from excessive red tape, regulatory uncertainty, and an ideological attack.

The bill would require employers to check existing super funds via the ATO when a new employee does not nominate one, mandate annual APRA performance tests for funds, and prohibit persistently underperforming funds from accepting new members after two years, with the aim of saving Australians $14 billion over a decade. It also clarifies trustees’ obligations to act solely in members’ financial interests.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 gives the Treasurer unilateral power to cancel investments, a measure the speaker called illiberal and dangerous, and argued it fails to reduce superannuation fees while potentially locking up to three million Australians into underperforming funds costing $635,000 less in retirement.

The speaker supported schedules 1 and 2 of the bill—which staple super accounts to employees and introduce annual performance testing—but opposed schedule 3, arguing its “best financial interests” covenant, reversal of the burden of proof, and regulation-making power allowing the Treasurer to ban investments could harm members and were not recommended by reviews. They called on the government to rethink schedule 3 and re-engage with stakeholders.

The independent MP announced they will oppose the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, primarily because schedule 3 gives the Treasurer broad unilateral powers over super fund investments; they support other schedules subject to amendments including delaying stapling until after two years of performance testing and applying the performance test to all funds equally.

The Morrison government's Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 aims to save Australians $17.9 billion over 10 years by limiting multiple superannuation accounts, requiring annual performance tests for super products, and tightening trustee duties to act in members' best financial interests.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021 for introducing a single default fund, transparency on underperforming funds, and a best-interest duty, and argued Labor opposed it to protect union funding and influence.

The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, arguing it would allow workers to be stapled to underperforming superannuation funds, replace trustees’ duty to act in members’ best interests with a narrower “best financial interests” standard that could discourage long-term community investments, and give the Treasurer excessive power via unfinished regulations—reflecting what the speaker described as a government ideological attack on industry superannuation, despite industry funds outperforming retail funds and the royal commission finding widespread abuse in retail funds only.

The speaker gave qualified support for the Treasury Laws Amendment (Your Future, Your Super) Bill 2021, urging amendments such as sequencing to eliminate poor-performing funds before the stapling provision begins, extending annual performance tests to all superannuation products not just MySuper, and setting a financial threshold on best‑financial‑interest provisions to avoid unnecessary administrative costs. They welcomed the removal of the directions power and specifically opposed the use of compulsory superannuation for political donations, advertising at sporting events, or corporate box hire.

The Morrison government's Your Future, Your Super Bill implements Productivity Commission and banking royal commission recommendations to prevent multiple super accounts, empower member choice, penalise underperforming funds, and increase transparency, projected to save Australians nearly $18 billion over 10 years.

The government introduced the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill to create a framework for independently authorised cross-border data requests from designated communications providers, enabling a bilateral CLOUD Act agreement with the United States and reciprocal assistance for partner countries. The bill includes safeguards such as provider objection rights, oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman and Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, and annual ministerial reports to parliament.

The speaker supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020, noting the government agreed to 23 bipartisan amendments from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, but criticised the Morrison government for being slow to negotiate a CLOUD Act agreement with the United States and accused the Prime Minister of falsely claiming the bill lacked bipartisan support.

The Greens argued that the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020 lacks adequate protections and safeguards, including for human rights, journalists' data, and parliamentary scrutiny, with critical details left to future international agreements and concerns about the Administrative Appeals Tribunal issuing orders instead of the judiciary.

The speaker opposed the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (International Production Orders) Bill 2020, arguing it was being rushed through Parliament without adequate debate. They noted that over 80 national security laws have been passed since 9/11 and called for the bill to be delayed until the next day for full consideration.

The bill creates a framework for international production orders to obtain electronic data from foreign communications providers, aiming to reduce delays in international cooperation for serious crime investigations, and its passage is a critical step to finalising a bilateral CLOUD Act agreement with the United States.
